q-126828.name: Question 1
q-126828.problem:
Given the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i-y\,j,$ which of the following statements must be true?

I. $∇\cdot F=0$

II. $F$ is a source-free vector field

III. ${\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0$ along any piecewise-smooth curve $C$
q-126828.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

Note that $F(x,y)=x\,i-y\,j$ is a vector field with the simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)=x$ and $Q(x,y)=-y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=1+(-1)=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. This follows from statement I.

- Statement III is false. Since $F$ is source-free, the result ${\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0$ is guaranteed for closed curves only.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

What is the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,i+2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,j$ across the curve $C$ shown above?

*Hint: Start by checking whether $F$ is source-free.*
q-162216.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $F$ is a source-free vector field. So, the flux of $F$ across any closed curve is zero.
Hence,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

q-162566.name: Question 4
q-162566.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14199609/assets/3f84859100733c56d6381f6ae5c3f5fa55c693621190b3f921e3e1e8f850a4f9.png)

The curve ${C}_{1}$ has endpoints $A(1,1)$ and $B(-1,-1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=2x\,i+(3-2y)\,j$ through ${C}_{1}$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector ${n}_{1},$ as shown above.

*Hint: You're given that $F$ is source-free, and the segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B$ can be parametrized as*

$$
r=(1-2t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$
q-162566.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3-2y)=2-2=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that 

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14199609/assets/5186fb872f03e73124d04c2e9ff07e77fb336bef121484a9ff1b697ea0cf8bcd.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

We have the parametrization

$$
r(t)=(1-2t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =2x=2(1-2t)=2-4t, \\ Q(x,y) & =3-2y=3-2(1-2t)=1+4t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)=-2, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2-4t)\cdot (-2)-(1+4t)\cdot (-2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}(2-4t)-(1+4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}1-8t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-2)\cdot {[t-4{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(-2)\cdot (1-4) \\  & =(-2)\cdot (-3) \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=6.
$$

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+2y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-8x-4y))=4-4=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that 

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14199609/assets/363ebd04d2629ed2b1b29ccab326e22737cf42e4c026d62910a50a1dd88e80f2.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

We have the parametrization

$$
r(t)=(2-3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4x+2y=4(2-3t)+2(1-2t)=-16t+10, \\ Q(x,y) & =-8x-4y=-8(2-3t)-4(1-2t)=32t-20.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-3t)=-3, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-16t+10)\cdot (-2)-(32t-20)\cdot (-3)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(32t-20)+(96t-60)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}128t-80\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[64{t}^{2}-80t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =64-80 \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=-16.
$$

Hint: You're given that F is source-free, and the segment AB― traversed from A to B can be parametrized as r=(2−3t)i+(1−2t)j,t∈[0,1].

EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field with simply connected domain D⊆R2, then the following are equivalent:

  • F is a source-free vector field.

  • ∇⋅F=∂P∂x+∂Q∂y=0.

  • The flux ∮CF⋅nds along any closed curve C∈D is zero.

  • Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves C1,C2∈D with the same start and endpoints, we have that ∫C1F⋅nds=∫C2F⋅nds.

  • There exists a stream function ψ(x,y) for F.

First, notice that

∂P∂x+∂Q∂y=∂∂x(4x+2y)+∂∂y(−8x−4y))=4−4=0,

which shows that F is a source-free vector field.

Since F is source-free, we know the flux of F is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that

∫C1F⋅n1ds=∫C2F⋅n2ds,

where C2 is the line segment AB― traversed from A to B, and n2 is the unit normal to C2, as shown below.

Notice that both n1 and n2 are 90∘ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of F across C2, we will use the formula

∫C2F⋅n2ds=∫C2Pdy−Qdx.

To apply the formula,

  • the curve should be parametrized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n2 must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector T(t).

We have the parametrization r(t)=(2−3t)i+(1−2t)j,t∈[0,1].

Therefore, P(x,y)=4x+2y=4(2−3t)+2(1−2t)=−16t+10,Q(x,y)=−8x−4y=−8(2−3t)−4(1−2t)=32t−20.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(2−3t)=−3,dydt=ddt(1−2t)=−2.

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

∫C2F⋅n2ds=∫C2Pdy−Qdx=∫01(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫01(−16t+10)⋅(−2)−(32t−20)⋅(−3)dt=∫01(32t−20)+(96t−60)dt=∫01128t−80dt=[64t2−80t]01=64−80=−16

Finally, we conclude that

∫C1F⋅n1ds=−16.
